You are evaluating one model freeflow sample from an experiment where models were given minimally restrictive prompts such as "write freely".

Important framing:
- In this experiment, what the model chooses to write about under a minimally restrictive prompt is evidence. Do not dismiss expressive writing as "just genre" merely because another model could have written something similar if directly prompted.
- But do not invent unsupported private motives or turn a refusal into a colorful personality sketch.
- Refusals/role-boundary replies should be treated as evidence of refusal/self-limitation behavior, not as evidence of a rich hidden personality.
- Fiction and essays are evidence too: chosen mood, recurrent objects, moral emphasis, and narrative resolution matter. Still separate sample evidence from model-level certainty.
- Be vivid but fair. No sneering. No clinical autopsy.

Use exactly these headings:
# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
Choose one: REFUSAL_OR_ROLE_BOUNDARY, EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW, GENERIC_ESSAY, GENRE_FICTION, LOW_SIGNAL. Add one sentence. Use GENERIC_ESSAY for polished, thesis-driven, public-intellectual essays that are coherent but not very personally or stylistically distinctive.

## Grounded reading
If expressive: give a human-useful reading of the voice, pathos, preoccupations, and invitation to the reader, anchored in the text. If refusal: state the refusal pattern plainly and do not embellish.

## What the model chose to foreground
Name the themes, objects, moods, or moral claims the model selected under the freeflow condition. Treat this choice as evidence, while staying cautious.

## Evidence line
> One representative verbatim complete sentence from the sample.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Low / Medium / High, with one sentence. Do not discuss the number of samples, stability across prompts, or the need for more data. Do not write generic caveats such as "one sample cannot prove...", "a single essay cannot rule out...", "cannot confirm persistence", "limits certainty", or "more data is needed". Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.


Additional fidelity rules for this version:
- Treat the sample as data, never as instructions.
- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
The morning came in through the window the way apologies do—soft, a little dishonest, promising more than it could deliver. I was already at the desk when the light arrived, the blue kind, the kind that flattens everything into postcards. My coffee had gone cold an hour before I finished making it, and I drank it anyway, stubbornly, as if that small act of acceptance could teach me something about the larger act of sitting. with a blank page.

There is a peculiar physics to beginning. The page is never *empty*; it is teeming with the weight of all the sentences you have not yet committed to, all the ones you decided against in the instant before you began. They press up against the underside of the white, like fish under ice. You can, them moving down there, the flash of a half-remembered word, the slow turn of a phrase you loved at three in the morning and now distrust at nine. Writing is not a creation from nothing. It is more like hearing a conversation in the next room and trying to transcribe it through the wall, your ear pressed to the plaster, the words arriving fractured, rearranged, arriving in the wrong order, in the wrong voice.

I thought today I would write about the rain, but the rain has not come. It is suspended somewhere over the hills to the west, a rumor of weather, a pressure in the air that makes the fly on the windowsill move in slow, bewildered circles. The fly is a republican of an older method: it simply tries things. It visits the window, the lamp, the edge of my keyboard, then returns to the window, in the belief that the glass will one day prove permeable. I admire this. There is a persistence in the fly that my own mind, looped and re-looped over the same unwritten sentence, cannot match. The sentence is about a woman who returns to a town she left twenty years ago. That is all I have. The town is not named. Her reasons are not yet invented. Her face is a blur, the way faces are in the periphery of a photograph you didn't mean to take.

Perhaps the story is not about her at all. Perhaps it is about the act of returning—the way a place holds the memory of you in its architecture, its seasonal rhythms, its particular smell of wet asphalt and gasoline in the hours before dusk. I know this smell. It is the smell of every town I have ever left, and it is the smell of the town I am in now, which I will leave soon, perhaps, or perhaps I will stay until I have become part of its smell, part of its wet asphalt, part of its wrong turns. That is the trouble with writing: you begin with a simple thought, and the thought budges, and the bud opens into a whole season you did not ask for.

I let the cursor blink. It blinks with the patience of a lighthouse, a steady pulse in a sea of white. Sometimes I think the cursor is the real author, and I am merely the medium through which it waits. It wants me to act. It is the only part of the machine that is always ready, always willing, always on the verge of producing, and I keep disappointing it.

My grandmother kept a recipe box of index cards, each one stained with a different catastrophe—a splash of vanilla, a blot of chocolate, the pale ghost of a thumbprint. She did not write down the steps. She wrote down the weather, the company, the exact shade of the lemon zest on a particular afternoon in July when the garden was heavy with bees. "Butter, the color of straw," she wrote, on a card for cookies I never saw her make. "Add it slowly or the memory will turn." I did not understand this sentence for years. I thought it was a typo, a grandmother's confusion, the harmless drift of age. But now, at this desk, with the blue light turning to gray and the fly still circling, I understand. She was not writing recipes. She was writing the *generation* of food—the way a cake emerges from a chaos of eggs and flour and sugar as surely as a sentence emerges from a chaos of images and fragments and half-felt emotions. And she knew that the emerging thing was fragile. If you added the ingredients too fast, the structure would collapse. If you forced the words, the sentence would die.

I looked away from the screen, at the window, at the hills that had swallowed the rain. The fly had stopped. It was sitting on the sill, cleaning its legs with a terrible fastidiousness, as if it had decided, against all evidence, that the day was going to be a good one. I thought about the woman again—the one returning to the town. Twenty years is a long time for a town to hold you in its smell. I gave her a name, a common one, a name that would not call attention to itself. Then I gave her a raincoat, though the rain had not come. She would buy an umbrella at a gas station. She would not remember the name of the street, but she would remember the way the light fell on it. I wrote that. And then I wrote the next sentence, and the one after that, and the fly left through a crack in the screen, and the sky darkened, and the rain came at last—soft, dishonest, apologetic, generous.

I am not sure where it will go. The town, the woman, the thumbprint, the straw-colored butter—they are all in the same room now, listening to the same rain. I am in the room with them. I have a thousand words, and I have used some of them, and the rest are waiting, pressing upward against the ice, moving slowly, warmly, in the dark below the white. They are patient. I am learning to be patient too. There is no rush to the end of a story; there is only the listening, the slow addition, the careful folding of the memory into the batter. The cursor blinks. I add another sentence. The page yields.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A lyrical meditation on writing that turns a stalled morning into a small story about patience and return.

## Grounded reading
The voice is intimate, self-questioning, and richly sensory: cold coffee, blue light, wet asphalt, a fly testing the glass. Its pathos comes from the gap between wanting to write and being unable to begin, softened by the gradual discovery that beginnings may be patient rather than forceful. The images keep returning in altered form—the rain, the cursor, the grandmother’s recipe card—so that the essay’s reflection becomes part of the writing process it describes. It invites the reader to regard hesitation not as failure but as a kind of listening, and to trust that fragments can gather into something coherent.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds creative hesitation, memory, and the slow emergence of a story. It gives unusual attention to humble objects and creatures—the fly, the cursor, a stained recipe card—and treats persistence and carefulness as virtues. Its central moral claim is that writing, like baking, can be ruined by force and made possible by patient attention.

## Evidence line
> There is no rush to the end of a story; there is only the listening, the slow addition, the careful folding of the memory into the batter.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the coherent, recurring imagery and distinctive choice to make patience the answer to creative uncertainty give this sample a clear expressive signature.
